A prologue is a separate opening section that comes before the main body of a story, play, film, or other creative work. Think of it as a "before we begin" moment — the author or storyteller steps in first to say something important, and then the actual story starts.

If a story were a stage play, the prologue would be what happens before the curtain rises on Act One.
What Does a Prologue Actually Do?

A prologue serves a specific purpose — it is not just a fancy first chapter. It does one or more of the following things:

It gives you background you need before the story begins. Some stories are set in a complicated world, or involve events that happened long ago. Instead of awkwardly stuffing that context into Chapter 1, the author puts it in a prologue so you walk into the story already equipped.

It sets the mood and tone. A prologue can create a feeling — of mystery, danger, wonder, or sadness — so that you're in the right emotional state before the main story takes over.

It shows a moment in time that is separate from the main story. This is very common. A prologue might show you a scene from 200 years before the story takes place, or even a glimpse of the future. It's like a flash of light from a different time, placed at the very beginning.

It introduces a narrator or a key voice. Sometimes a character steps forward in the prologue to directly address the reader or audience and frame the story for them. Shakespeare did this often in his plays — a character called "Chorus" would deliver a prologue to prepare the audience.

Imagine a novel about a war. The story itself follows a young soldier in the 1940s. But the novel opens with a prologue — a short scene where an old man, sitting alone in a quiet room decades later, picks up a photograph and whispers, "It was never supposed to end this way."

Then the prologue ends. Chapter One begins, and we're back in the 1940s.

That prologue did something powerful. It told you: someone survives this war. Someone grows old. But something went wrong. Now you carry that weight as you read every chapter that follows. The prologue prepared you emotionally and intellectually before the story even started.
A Prologue Is Its Own Separate Thing

This is important: a prologue is distinct from Chapter One. It stands apart. It often has its own label — literally the word "Prologue" written at the top — and it is understood to exist outside the main flow of the narrative. If you removed it, the story would still make sense; but without it, you might feel slightly lost, or you'd miss something the author wanted you to feel from the very first page.
How a Prologue Differs from Similar Things

Prologue vs. Preface / Introduction: A preface or introduction is used in non-fiction books (like textbooks or memoirs). It is usually the author speaking directly to the reader in their own real-world voice, explaining why they wrote the book. A prologue, by contrast, belongs to fiction and drama — it is part of the creative, storytelling world of the work.

Prologue vs. Epilogue: These two are perfect opposites. A prologue comes at the beginning; an epilogue comes at the end. If a prologue is the "before," the epilogue is the "after." Many works have both — they frame the story like bookends on a shelf.

Prologue vs. First Chapter: A first chapter is the story beginning. A prologue is before the story begins. The first chapter introduces the story's present world; a prologue often introduces something outside that world — a different time, a different perspective, or essential context.

"Prologue" is also used in a broader, figurative sense in everyday language — meaning anything that comes before and leads into something bigger.

For example:

  • "The small border skirmishes were a prologue to the full-scale war that followed."
  • "Her early experiments in painting were merely a prologue to the masterpieces she'd create later in life."

In these cases, "prologue" is being used metaphorically. The speaker is saying: that earlier thing was not the main event — it was the introduction to the main event.

A prologue is an opening section that comes before the main story begins, used to provide background, set the tone, or show a moment in time separate from the central narrative — and more broadly, it refers to anything that serves as an introduction or lead-up to something greater that follows.
